item.title: Robot's viral 'face-covering' sprint at 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games is 'spontaneous,' not designed by developers
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 11:42:00
Tien Kung Omni humanoid robots sprint at the 400-meter run small-group final at the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games held in Beijing on August 23, 2026. Photo: Tao Mingyang/GT A humanoid robot that grabbed a 400-meter title at the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games (WHRG) in Beijing while appearing to "cover its face with both hands" developed the unusual posture by itself during sprinting, its developers said, after clips of the run drew wide attention online. Tien Kung Omni, built by the Beijing-based X-Humanoid, won the 400-meter run small-group final on Sunday in 45.66 seconds. Rather than swinging its arms forward and back as a human sprinter does, the robot ran with its center of gravity pitched forward and its arms held high near its face, swinging them widely as its hips rotated from side to side — a gait viewers likened to "a shy person hiding behind their hands." The posture was not what engineers had in mind. "We initially designed Tien Kung Omni's gait around a human-style arm swing," Han Gang, a motion control algorithm expert at the company, told the Global Times. In a simulated learning environment, the team gave the robot continuous rewards, and through repeated iteration on the data it gradually settled into a posture that suited it better. "It feels that this is more comfortable," Han said. The reason is a physical constraint, Han explained. Swinging the arms rapidly places a heavy load on the shoulder joints, which can cause them to heat up and drive up energy consumption — leaving the robot unable to sustain the full 400m. Running with its hands near its face allows the robot to complete the distance quickly while keeping its legs powerful and its arms under low load. Different distances pose different problems, Han added. In endurance events such as the humanoid half-marathon, engineers have to pay closer attention to heat dissipation in the hip joints after long periods of running. Over shorter distances such as the 100m and 400m, hip overload is much less of a concern. The next challenge, Han said, lies beyond the track: robots will need to interact with more complex environments and complete tasks while being disturbed by outside forces. "Once there is a breakthrough, we may soon see unexpected applications across many fields," he said. In the large-group 400-meter run final held earlier the same day, the company's Tien Kung Ultra took gold in 38.15 seconds. The time is faster than the men's 400m world record of 43.03 seconds, set by South Africa's Wayde van Niekerk at the 2016 Rio Olympics and still standing after a decade. The margin reflects how quickly the field is moving. At the first edition of the games last year, the winning 400m time was 1 minute 28.03 seconds — nearly 50 seconds slower. Global Times

item.title: Chinese-founded fast-fashion retailer Shein seeks to raise $1.8 billion in Hong Kong IPO
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 10:21:00
Photo: VCG Chinese-founded fast-fashion retailer Shein is seeking to raise HK$13.9 billion ($1.8 billion) in its IPO at the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, as the company's shares are expected to commence trading on September 1, according to a filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange on Monday. The company is offering 280 million shares at HK$47.6 to HK$49.5 per share. Institutional investors include Boyu Capital, Tiger Global, General Atlantic, and Tencent Holdings Ltd. Shein said that it plans to use the IPO proceeds to enhance technological capabilities such as the procurement of cloud and server services, invest in marketing to enhance brand awareness and expand global footprint, and strengthen its supply chain governance and ensure compliance with evolving regulations across various jurisdictions related to sustainability and corporate responsibility. Founded in 2012, Shein has grown into a global fast-fashion e-commerce platform serving 273 million active customers in approximately 160 markets in 2025. According to a report from consulting firm GlobalData, Shein surpassed Zara, H&M, and Uniqlo in 2024 to become the third-largest player in the global apparel market, just behind Nike and Adidas. In July, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) approved Shein to proceed with its Hong Kong IPO, according to a notice seen on the CSRC website on July 10.

item.title: Two Chinese sailors rescued, 22 missing after Panama-flagged bulk carrier sinks off eastern India's coast
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 10:16:00
Caption: The Indian Coast Guard and the Indian Navy have launched a joint rescue operation after the Panama-flagged bulk carrier Ocean Winner sank in waters off the coast of Paradip, India's Odisha state. Photo: Screenshot of NDTV's report Two Chinese sailors have been rescued after a Panama-flagged bulk carrier carrying 24 crew members sank in the Bay of Bengal, about 230 nautical miles off the coast of Paradip, India's Odisha state, as Indian authorities intensified search-and-rescue operations for the remaining 22 crew members, according to multiple Indian media outlets and Reuters. The two sailors were rescued from life rafts by MT Aisopos, a commercial vessel operating nearby, after an Indian Navy P-8I maritime surveillance aircraft located the rafts during the search-and-rescue mission, the Times of India reported. The two Chinese seafarers said the vessel, called Ocean Winner, had developed a list on Friday and sank within eight minutes, forcing the crew to abandon ship, Reuters reported, citing Shyam Jagannathan, director general of India's Maritime Administration. Jagannathan said the chances of finding survivors generally fall sharply after the first 12 hours, but rescuers were continuing their search. Ocean Winner, with IMO number 9145530, was a 70,000-deadweight-ton bulk carrier built in 1998. It loaded iron ore at Paradip and departed for Singapore on Thursday with 24 crew members aboard, according to Maritime Executive. The vessel's Automatic Identification System signal disappeared in the middle of the Bay of Bengal at 4:45 pm GMT on Friday. The crew issued a distress alert at around the same time, the report said. The 22 missing crew members include 18 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi, according to the Indian Coast Guard. Two Coast Guard vessels were dispatched from Sri Vijaya Puram, formerly known as Port Blair and the capital of India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands, to join the search-and-rescue operation, according to a Coast Guard spokesperson cited by Reuters. Separately, Maritime Executive noted that iron ore fines can become hazardous when wet, as the cargo may liquefy and suddenly shift to one side while a vessel is rolling. This induces a list, accompanied by free surface effect, with serious adverse impact on stability. From 2007 to 2019, 29 seafarers were killed in casualties involving iron ore cargoes, the outlet reported. Global Times

item.title: Chinese-built highway opens ahead of schedule in Senegal
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 09:12:00
Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye (4th R) addresses the opening ceremony of the Mbour-Kaolack highway project in Thiadiaye, Mbour Department, in Senegal's western Thies Region, Aug. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Qi Qi) The Mbour-Kaolack highway project, built by China Road and Bridge Corporation, opened to traffic on Saturday at a ceremony in Thiadiaye, Mbour Department, in Senegal's western Thies Region. Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye (3rd R) unveils a plaque of the Mbour-Kaolack highway project in Thiadiaye, Mbour Department, in Senegal's western Thies Region, Aug. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Qi Qi) Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye attended the ceremony and said the highway reflects the "quality of the relations between Senegal and China." He said the project is "particularly important for facilitating travel" in central Senegal and improving connectivity between the central region and other parts of the country. "The highway, which was due to be delivered at the end of September, is now open to traffic," Faye said. The president thanked the Chinese side for its support and expressed his willingness to further deepen bilateral relations and advance cooperation with China. Stretching 99.2 km, the Mbour-Kaolack highway connects the western coastal city of Mbour with Kaolack in central Senegal.

item.title: China's global initiatives offer new opportunities for cooperation, says Italian business leader
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 08:50:00
Guests attend the 4th China-Italy Friendship Cities Cooperation Dialogue in Rome, Italy, April 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Jing) The China-proposed four global initiatives offer a new perspective on international governance and new opportunities for international cooperation amid geopolitical fragmentation and global instability, said an Italian business leader. The initiatives represent China's efforts to provide coordinated responses to challenges that transcend national borders, Mario Boselli, president of the Italy-China Foundation, said in a recent interview with Xinhua. They also represent a deepening of China's international vision following more than a decade of the Belt and Road Initiative, extending the focus from economic and infrastructure cooperation to development, security, dialogue among civilizations and global governance, he said. He believes that the Global Development Initiative (GDI) and the Global Civilization Initiative (GCI) could offer opportunities to deepen cooperation between China and Europe, including Italy. The GDI's focus on climate change, the UN Sustainable Development Goals, digitalization and technological innovation could create opportunities for cooperation in renewable energy, photovoltaics and energy storage, among others, said Boselli. Italy and China can also strengthen cooperation among universities and research institutions in biotechnology, healthcare, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing, he added. Noting that the GCI could promote cooperation in culture, heritage conservation, universities and youth exchanges, he said Italy, with its rich cultural heritage and the strong appeal of "Made in Italy" in China, is "one of the most natural European partners" for such initiatives. Taken together, the four initiatives outline a vision of a multipolar world with greater participation by emerging economies and countries of the Global South, Boselli said. With its tradition of dialogue with China and complementary economic strengths, Italy can play a bridging role between China and Europe, promoting practical cooperation in sustainable development, innovation, culture and global governance, he said. China's initiatives may not provide an immediate solution to current international tensions, but can offer "a space for reflection and dialogue" to identify more inclusive, practical and long-term forms of cooperation, he added.

item.title: Tanzanian president inaugurates Julius Nyerere Hydropower Plant
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 08:32:00
Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan addresses the inauguration ceremony of the Julius Nyerere Hydropower Plant in Coast Region, Tanzania, Aug. 22, 2026. Hassan on Saturday inaugurated the 2,115-megawatt Julius Nyerere Hydropower Plant, a landmark project expected to strengthen electricity supply and accelerate industrial and economic development. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman) Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan on Saturday inaugurated the 2,115-megawatt Julius Nyerere Hydropower Plant, a landmark project expected to strengthen electricity supply and accelerate industrial and economic development. Hassan inaugurated the plant in Rufiji District in Coast Region, saying the new generation capacity should produce measurable gains in manufacturing, trade, mining, modern agriculture, public services, investment and employment. The nine-unit facility now accounts for nearly half of electricity dispatched to Tanzania's national grid, significantly improving reliability and security of supply, she said. "This project has demonstrated Tanzania's capabilities. We must now harness that capacity to advance other strategic projects and build a strong, self-reliant nation," Hassan said. Built with the participation of China's Power Construction Corporation of China (PowerChina) and Dongfang Electric Corporation, the plant has a total installed capacity of 2,115 megawatts, Zhang Rui, the project manager with PowerChina, said. PowerChina undertook the construction of the main works, including the main dam, the stilling basin, the water conveyance system, the diversion tunnels and the metal structures, as well as the overall engineering design and the supporting facilities, Zhang said. Tan Jin, the project manager with Dongfang Electric, noted that they supplied all nine hydro-turbine generator units, main inlet valves and other complete sets of electromechanical equipment, and carried out their installation, commissioning and trial operation. During construction, the China-involved construction work created about 14,000 jobs for local residents. Thousands of Tanzanians received professional skills training from Chinese engineers in areas such as welding, steel fixing, carpentry, heavy machinery operation and surveying, helping build a stronger local workforce, according to the two managers. The project is also expected to improve electricity supply for households and public services, strengthen Tanzania's role in the regional energy market in East Africa, and provide reliable energy support for regional connectivity and socioeconomic development, said Humphrey Moshi, an economics professor at the University of Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. item.title: Tight hug after 27 years: Reunion across ocean, marking China-US folk friendship
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 23:54:00
Tight hug after 27 years: Reunion across ocean, marking China-US folk friendship By Lin Xiaoyi in Ordos and Zhang Han in Beijing Published: Aug 23, 2026 11:54 PM American teacher Ronald Sakolsky reunites with desert fighter Yin Yuzhen at an airport in Ordos, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region on August 23, 2026. Photo: Xinhua A long-awaited reunion that captured wide public attention unfolded on Sunday evening when American teacher Ronald Sakolsky and Yin Yuzhen, a model worker renowned for planting trees and combating desertification, reunited and embraced tearfully with overwhelming emotion at an airport in Ordos, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, after 27 years of separation across the ocean. The reunion began with a single act of generosity in 1999. When Sakolsky arrived in China as a participant in a China-US education exchange program, he was moved by Yin and her husband's tireless efforts to curb desertification in the Mu Us Desert in Inner Mongolia. He raised $5,000 to fund their local tree-planting initiative. The young saplings they bought with the donation have since matured into more than 50,000 full-grown trees, transforming the once desolate, sandy wasteland into a thriving green landscape. This hug, transcending time and distance, marked not only friendship between the two countries, but also showcased the sincerity of Chinese people and a green miracle made possible through continuous joint efforts. Seeds of China-US friendship sown long ago, now stand as towering woods. Illustration: Liu Rui/GT Hug across 27 years At 2:48 am on early Sunday morning, Ronald Sakolsky arrived at Beijing Capital International Airport after over 10 hours of flight. As he stepped into the arrivals hall, he greeted the waiting reporters with earnest Putonghua "Wo hui lai le," meaning "I'm back." "When I saw the lights in Beijing as we were landing is when I realized that I am back in my second home." Asked what he is most looking forward to about this journey, Sakolsky told the Global Times that "I want to see Ms Yin, see the forests, see the students I have not seen for almost 30 years, my colleagues. I want to see the Chinese people." He then flew to Ordos for the meeting with his desert reclamation partner. Yin waited at the arrival gate at the airport in Ordos very early, murmuring English sentence she particularly learned for this occasion - "Welcome to China, my brother." Her eyes were fixed on the escalator and she wiped away her tears multiple times during the wait, the Global Times reporter observed. Sakolsky said in earlier interview with the Global Times that he was looking forward to this reunion and could not hold his tears back when he thought of the moment. He was about to give Yin a hug when they meet. When Sakolsky finally appeared in front of Yin, their eyes welled up. Stepping off the elevator, Sakolsky could barely contain his excitement, muttering "Oh my God, oh my God." They hurried toward each other and locked in a tight embrace at last - the long-awaited hug 27 years in the making. "This is a dream come true, from a lady who is the hero of the story, not me," Sakolsky told the Global Times at the airport, barely holding his emotion. "She made a promise 27 years ago, and she kept her promise." Talking about his donation almost three decades ago, Sakolsky said the purpose was to help her, "because she was beautifying the motherland." Now, in response to an invitation to return to China for a trip to see the green planting from his donation and to returning to the city of Luoyang, Central China's Henan Province, where he taught in the exchange program for several years, Sakolsky noted that "China had done so much for me that I wanted to say thank you to China." A return of kindness For this reunion after 27 years, Yin had carefully prepared. Steamed buns, meaning "upward," fresh vegetables and fruits picked in the land transformed from desert. Yin, never familiar with any foreign language, learned some English phrases, including "welcome to China" she practiced, "my brother" to greet Sakolsky, and "more, more" to persuade the American friend to eat more. On Sunday, Yin did her hair and wore a red scarf alongside an outfit with a green shade, which she picked particularly for the reunion, as "green is the color of the Earth," as she told the Global Times. Yin is not the only old friend that was looking forward to the reunion. While Sakolsky was still on his over-10-hour flight from the US to Beijing, Bai Fan was also on the way - driving over 850 kilometers from Luoyang to Inner Mongolia. The journey would take a day and a half. Bai was the vice principal of Luoyang Foreign Language School, overseeing international affairs. Sakolsky was an exchange teacher there through a China-US program, and was Bai's "neighbor right across the hall." Why drive such a distance? Bai had prepared special cultural gifts - peony porcelain and Hanguan Kiln purple clay tea ware, distinctive local handicrafts that proved too bulky and fragile for air travel or high-speed rail. Bai recalled Sakolsky's continuous interest in Chinese culture, and sending a replica of Terracotta Warriors to the US at Sakolsky's request. "I hope he can take these Luoyang elements and Chinese symbols to the world," Bai told the Global Times in a phone interview on Sunday. Bai is also eager to see Sakolsky at a place that they had traveled together 27 years ago. When Sakolsky came to Luoyang for the exchange program, Bai was his designated liaison. Together, they traveled to the heart of the Mu Us Desert to deliver the $5,000 donation. Bai still vividly remembers the desolate desert back then, where finger-thin saplings were watered ladle by ladle by Yin. At that time, Sakolsky had constant concerns about whether the tiny saplings could survive in the wasteland, which makes today's sprawling 50,000-tree forest even more miraculous. The changed and unchanged Things have changed over the past 27 years. While waiting for Sakolsky, Yin jokingly said he got less hair, and she would not be able to recognize him if running up to him on street. The passage of time has brought far more than personal aging, according to Bai, another witness to the decades-long changes. "Everyone is growing older. Our families have expanded with more children, local communities have grown in population, and the surrounding environment is constantly evolving, just as our cities are undergoing profound transformations." On a night tour in Ordos on Sunday, Sakolsky, watching a fountain light show, said that "it is a 21st century city, but it looks like a 22nd century city. In the 2000s, Chinese government made a promise to Chinese people to beatify this country, and they succeeded." For Sakolsky, probably the most profound transformation lies in the depth of his human connection forged. "27 years ago, we were just friends and acquaintances. We are brother and sister now. So much has happened since then, but the important thing is many people have seen the story and now they can also help to make China beautiful," he told the reporters. Through joint efforts of people like Yin, the Mu Us Desert has turned from wasteland into a green oasis. China has contributed about 25 percent of the world's newly added green areas and taken the lead in achieving zero growth in land degradation, per official data. Meanwhile, there are things unchanged, including a vintage photo of the three standing in the desert that has decorated Bai's office through all these years - a permanent reminder of their original aspiration. This reunion will witness them retake the classic photo and plant new saplings together, expanding their green mission.

item.title: Canada launches a 'Chinese-styled counterattack' – a heavy blow: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 23:49:00
This combination of pictures created on August 22, 2026 shows US President Donald Trump in Washington, DC, on July 13, 2026 and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on August 22, 2026. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced retaliatory tariffs on the United States on August 22, after walking away from a "bad deal" on trade in a deepening rift between the longtime allies. Photo: VCG In the face of Washington's tariff stick, Canada has launched a "Chinese-styled counterattack": responding firmly and proportionally; defending sovereignty without compromise; and resorting to rules and legitimate countermeasures. As one of America's former closest allies, Canada's move reflects an increasingly clear consensus: No country has the privilege to monopolize the rules or dictate the fate of others. Washington probably never imagined that Ottawa would launch a "Chinese-styled counterattack." In response to the US 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced in a televised national address on Saturday that Canada would "match Washington's new tariffs dollar for dollar." Starting September 8, Canada will impose retaliatory tariffs on US sectors such as steel, dairy, home appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. Canada, a member of the Five Eyes alliance and NATO, has now dared to turn against Washington and respond with retaliatory tariffs. The significance of this move goes far beyond the scope of a North American trade dispute. The US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer disparagingly likened Canada's retaliation to "the kind of things that China would do." In an interview with US media, he claimed that after Washington introduced trade policies aimed at bringing production back home and protecting American jobs, "two countries in the world have retaliated against us: [the] People's Republic of China and Canada." China and Canada are the only countries daring to respond to US pressure with reciprocal measures. This indicates that the so-called "Chinese-styled counterattack" is, in fact, another term for "refusing to accept unilateral pressure." Canada's response offers the world a glimpse of what China has long stood for: responding firmly and proportionally; defending sovereignty without compromise; and resorting to rules and legitimate countermeasures. More accurately, this is not a uniquely Chinese approach, but rather the most fundamental principle of reciprocity in international trade. Canada's adoption of this path is no surprise. It is a legitimate response to unilateral bullying - raising a shield when faced with pressure. The "Chinese-styled counterattack" not only protects a country's own interests, but also safeguards the stability of global supply chains and the fairness of the international trading order. Canada's move shows that "strategic autonomy" is gradually evolving from a common aspiration of Global South countries into a real-world issue for US allies. More countries are realizing that concessions toward the US do not necessarily bring respect and stability, and only by having more partners, more markets and more room for independent choices can they gain the leverage for negotiation and the strength to protect themselves. Canada's decision to respond to the US in a "Chinese way" vividly illustrates a fact: In the face of a tariff stick, being an ally offers no "exemption." Today it is Canada; tomorrow it could be the EU, and the day after, Japan or South Korea. By listing China and Canada together as "retaliators," Greer acknowledges the failure of US policy - if the policy were truly "great," why would even one of its closest allies feel compelled to strike back? If a policy forces countries with different geopolitical positions and institutional systems to take countermeasures, then the question should not be "why are they acting like China," but rather "why is US policy producing more China-like responses." At a deeper level, Canada's "Chinese-styled counterattack" exposes the dilemma of unilateralism. Globalization is not a one-man show staged by the US, and industrial chains are deeply interconnected. The US wants to use tariff barriers to force production back home, yet ignores the basic economic factors of cost, efficiency and resource endowments. As one of the US largest trading partners, Canada sees hundreds and thousands of tons of goods crossing the border each day. In 2024, the two countries' average daily trade reached $2.5 billion, reflecting deeply integrated supply chains on both sides. By imposing tariffs, Washington is effectively cutting itself in the foot. Even Fox News, a conservative-leaning media outlet, published an article warning consumers that "your favorite cocktail could be an unexpected casualty of the trade fight," as Canadian whiskey is one of the commonly used base spirits for cocktails in US bars and restaurants. The so-called goal of "protecting American jobs" is, in plain terms, "America first, everyone else to the sidelines." And what has the result been? "First" has turned into isolation, and "bringing back" has turned into bleeding out. The so-called "correcting trade imbalances" has resulted in disrupted supply chains for domestic companies, with US ordinary consumers footing the bill and inflationary pressures remaining high. The US federal data shows that manufacturing companies reduced their workforce in each of the eight months that followed the "Liberation Day" tariffs. Even if tariff walls can "kill a thousand enemies," the self-inflicted damage is far from trivial. Canada's "Chinese-styled counterattack" is a heavy blow against protectionism. China's steadfast resistance to US unilateral tariffs was once described by some Western commentators as a "lone exception." Now that one of America's former closest allies has taken a similar path, this in itself is correcting the narrative over "who upholds the rules and who breaks them," while also demonstrating the necessity and legitimacy of China's reciprocal countermeasures. The essence of the "Chinese-styled counterattack" is an increasingly clear consensus: Openness must be built on equality, cooperation must be premised on mutual respect, and no country has the privilege to monopolize the rules or dictate the fate of others.

item.title: GT Voice: Protectionism is the last thing European automakers need
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 21:46:00
Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT Sebastian Lechner, state chairperson of the Christian Democratic Union in Germany's Lower Saxony, has called for the EU to quickly impose import tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars, Reuters reported on Friday. For some time, European media have reported that the European Commission plans to impose countervailing duties on such vehicles, which will amplify concerns over China-EU trade tensions. As the home to Volkswagen's global headquarters, Lower Saxony has been bearing the brunt of industrial restructuring amid the global energy transition. So, the politician's call for imposing tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars is essentially an attempt to curry favor with local manufacturers and local workers in exchange for gaining political support from them. But turning the operational pressure of local carmakers into political demand to erect trade barriers will not solve Germany's industrial problems. On the contrary, protectionism will almost certainly steer German auto sector further down the wrong path. For years, a number of European politicians and industry players have attributed the rapid growth of Chinese new-energy vehicles to the so-called "subsidies," hoping that erecting higher tariffs can shield European carmakers from global competition. Yet, the growing popularity of Chinese hybrid vehicles in the European market stems from nothing but their perfect alignment with the most pressing consumer demands. For starters, it's very expensive for ordinary European consumers to replace vehicles due to the persistently high prices of local cars. The EU has unveiled a plan to drop the ban on new combustion-engine cars from 2035, which would allow continued sales of non-electric vehicles including plug‑in hybrids (PHEVs). Market acceptance of PHEVs is relatively high in Europe. As a matter of fact, Chinese PHEVs have helped fill a critical market gap and provided European consumers with a pragmatic and affordable low-carbon mobility solution. Resorting to protection by imposing higher trade tariffs will deprive European consumers of the right to buy high-quality and cost-effective cars. If anything, the market performance following the EU's imposition of new tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) has already proven that trade protectionism only delivers limited effects in the long run. A report published by The Guardian revealed this month that despite EU tariffs of up to 35.3 percent on the EVs made by some Chinese manufacturers, on top of the standard 10-percent import duty, Chinese EV sales have still risen across Europe to hit a record high. The share of EVs sold by Chinese brands rose to 14.2 percent across western European markets - or one in every seven EVs - in the first five months of this year, according to Schmidt Automotive Research. Following a brief sales drop caused by tariff shocks, Chinese cars have quickly regained growth momentum, as their appeal to European consumers who favor affordable, high‑quality electric mobility has not changed. If the EU extends protectionist measure to Chinese PHEVs, European consumers will bear the full brunt of higher prices. Elevated prices could erase the new energy consumption push in Europe. The European auto market, which has just begun to show signs of recovery, will once again be dragged into a prolonged slump by protectionism. According to China Automotive News, more than 40 percent of the complete vehicles exported from China to the EU market come from joint ventures or wholly foreign‑owned factories in China. That means for every five cars shipped to Europe, roughly two are produced by European or other foreign manufacturers - including BMW and Mercedes‑Benz, all of which rely on China's mature supply chains to build highly competitive models and ship them back to Europe. Imposing punitive duties on these vehicles would raise their costs and disrupt their integrated production strategies. In addition, China's stance on tackling trade issues with the EU has always been clear. In May, a spokesperson from China's Ministry of Commerce said that China will take resolute countermeasures if the EU insists on imposing discriminatory restrictions on Chinese companies. Ultimately, the competitiveness of the global auto industry is never decided by tariffs. The race toward electrification and intelligence is one of technological innovation, supply‑chain efficiency, and cost control. Tariff pushes by certain politicians may win favor from local workers, yet they will trap Europe's automotive industry in a vicious cycle of protectionism. In the long run, such short-sighted moves will undermine the long-term vitality and competitiveness of European carmakers.

item.title: China's robots: Don't just watch, understand the industrial system
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 20:48:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT A Chinese humanoid robot clocked 9.39 seconds to beat the men's 100m world record of 9.58 seconds set by Usain Bolt. This feat, achieved during the opening ceremony of the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, quickly captured global headlines. The second World Humanoid Robot Games offered a vivid window into the country's fast-moving robotics industry. Images of humanoid machines running, balancing, navigating obstacles and performing coordinated tasks naturally attract attention. Such events reveal something significant: China has become exceptionally capable of translating advances in components, controls, software integration and manufacturing into physical machines that can be built, tested and improved at speed. The value of these competitions lies less in a single headline-grabbing performance than in the industrial system behind it. A humanoid robot on a track is the visible result of motors, reducers, sensors, batteries, structural materials, motion-control systems, embedded software, training data, assembly processes and field maintenance working together. China's advantage increasingly lies in its ability to coordinate the entire supply chain. It has a broad base of electronics and machinery suppliers, strong manufacturing capacity, dense industrial clusters, and a large pool of potential users willing to test robots in factories, warehouses, ports, shops, hospitals and service settings. Competitions can therefore serve as public demonstrations and stress tests for a wider ecosystem. This development has occurred amid expanding US restrictions on China's access to advanced technologies, particularly leading-edge semiconductors, high-performance computing equipment and certain software and manufacturing tools. These measures have had real effects. They raise costs, complicate supply chains and make it harder for Chinese firms to obtain some of the most advanced chips and technical capabilities. Robotics increasingly depends on artificial intelligence, high-performance processors and sophisticated development tools, and US containment policy has challenged China's robotics development. Yet the restrictions have not stopped China's robotics industry from growing. One reason is that industrial competitiveness is not determined by frontier chips alone. In many robotics applications, the decisive challenge is making a system reliable, affordable, maintainable and safe in real operating conditions. China's large and varied domestic market provides companies with unusually frequent opportunities to confront these challenges. A robot deployed in a logistics center, manufacturing workshop or pharmacy generates feedback that can improve design, software, hardware integration and service procedures. This creates a reinforcing cycle: More applications produce more operational data and experience; better products reduce costs and increase confidence; and lower costs support wider deployment. Scale matters as well. China's manufacturing ecosystem enables firms to move from prototype to small-batch production and then to larger-scale delivery relatively quickly. That process can accelerate learning not only for robot makers but also for suppliers of actuators, sensors, machine vision systems, batteries and precision components. The result is not simply a lower-cost version of foreign technology. It is a growing capacity to adapt products to diverse use cases and to iterate rapidly when products encounter real-world constraints. This has implications beyond China. As robots become more available and affordable, they can help manufacturers globally address labor shortages, improve workplace safety and raise productivity in repetitive or hazardous tasks. Chinese firms can contribute equipment, components and competitive pressure that expand the overall market and reduce barriers to adoption. In this sense, China's robotics progress may become part of a broader modernization of global manufacturing rather than a purely national achievement. However, a balanced assessment requires acknowledging the remaining gaps. The US retains major strengths in foundational artificial intelligence research, advanced semiconductors, computing platforms and software ecosystems. Japan and several European countries remain highly competitive in precision components, industrial reliability, specialized automation, safety systems and technical standards. China still faces challenges in certain high-end chips, core software, advanced sensors, precision parts, long-term reliability, and internationally recognized standards and certification. China's recent robotics events deserve attention because they illustrate a broader industrial fact. Despite external technological constraints, China has leveraged its domestic market, supply-chain depth, engineering talent and manufacturing scale to strengthen its position in robotics. Its advantage lies not in claiming technological supremacy in every category, but in its growing ability to turn innovation into deployment. If China can continue to close its remaining gaps while remaining open to global collaboration and standards, its robotics industry could become an important contributor to the next phase of worldwide industrial development.
